Generic E-Variables for Exact Sequential kk-Sample Tests that allow for Optional Stopping

Rosanne Turner    Alexander Ly    Peter Grünwald

Abstract

We develop 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables for testing whether two or more data streams come from the same source or not, and more generally, whether the difference between the sources is larger than some minimal effect size. These 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables lead to exact, nonasymptotic tests that remain safe, i.e. keep their type-I error guarantees, under flexible sampling scenarios such as optional stopping and continuation. In special cases our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables also have an optimal ‘growth’ property under the alternative. While the construction is generic, we illustrate it through the special case of k×2k\times 2 contingency tables, where we also allow for the incorporation of different restrictions on a composite alternative. Comparison to p-value analysis in simulations and a real-world example show that 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables, through their flexibility, often allow for early stopping of data collection — thereby retaining similar power as classical methods — while also retaining the option of extending or combining data afterwards.

Keywords

E-values, Hypothesis testing, Sequential test, Type-I error control, Composite hypothesis, Test martingale

1 Introduction

We develop hypothesis tests that are robust under flexible sampling scenarios, in which one is allowed to engage in optional continuation and optional stopping. We focus on the setting with data coming from several groups, the goal being to test whether the underlying distributions are all the same or not. Since it considerably simplifies notation and treatment, we focus on two-sample tests throughout the paper, pointing out at the relevant places how to extend our results to the kk-sample setting for k>2k>2. Our methods are based on 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variables and test martingales. While to some extent going back as far as Darling and Robbins, (1967), interest in these concepts has exploded only very recently, in part in relation to the ongoing replicability crisis in the applied sciences (Howard et al.,, 2021; Ramdas et al.,, 2020; Vovk and Wang,, 2021; Shafer,, 2021; Grünwald et al.,, 2022; Pace and Salvan,, 2019; Manole and Ramdas,, 2021; Henzi and Ziegel,, 2021).

Thus, suppose we collect samples from two distinct groups, denoted aa and bb. In both groups, data are i.i.d. and come in sequentially — even though, as explained underneath (1.1) below, our approach can also be fruitfully used in the fixed design case. We thus have two data streams, Y1,a,Y2,a,…Y_{1,a},Y_{2,a},\ldots i.i.d. ∼Pθa\sim P_{\theta_{a}} and Y1,b,Y2,b,…Y_{1,b},Y_{2,b},\ldots i.i.d. ∼Pθb\sim P_{\theta_{b}} with θa,θb∈Θ\theta_{a},\theta_{b}\in\Theta, {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} representing some parameterized underlying family of distributions, all assumed to have a probability density or mass function denoted by pθp_{\theta} on some outcome space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. We will use notation P(θa,θb)P_{(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})} (density p(θa,θb)p_{(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})}) to represent the joint distribution of both streams. We consider a testing scenario, in which the null hypothesis ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} expresses that θa=θb{\theta_{a}}={\theta_{b}} and the alternative ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} expresses that d⁡(θa,θb)>δd(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})>\delta for some divergence measure dd and some effect size δ≥0\delta\geq 0. We design a family of tests for this scenario that preserve type-I error guarantees under optional stopping. Hence, if the level α\alpha-test is performed and the null hypothesis holds true, the probability that the null will ever be rejected is bounded by α\alpha. Our tests can be implemented, and are exact, for arbitrary {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} and in combination with arbitrary divergence measures dd. To our knowledge such a general construction is entirely new. For purposes of illustration and insight we choose to apply it to a very simple, classical problem: 2×22\times 2 contingency tables, with, in Section 5, an extension to k×2k\times 2 tables. As is well-known (for completeness we provide simulations demonstrating this in the supporting information), if a standard fixed-design method for this scenario, the p-value resulting from Fisher’s exact test, is (ab)used with optional stopping, the type-I error blows up. In contrast, our tests retain type-I error guarantee while, due to the optional stopping, having power competitive with Fisher’s p-value. In fact, in the k×2k\times 2 application (but not in general) our test has a GRO11 1 Nonstandard abbreviations: GRO: growth-rate optimal; REGROW: relative growth-rate optimality in worst-case (growth-rate optimal) property, GRO being the analogue of ’optimal power’ in our optional continuation setting.

Our test depends on the choice of a prior distribution on the alternative ℋ1={P(θa,θb):(θa,θb)∈Θ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})}:(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})\in\Theta_{1}\} with Θ1⊂{(θa,θb):θa,θb∈Θ}\Theta_{1}\subset\{(\theta_{a},\theta_{b}):\theta_{a},\theta_{b}\in\Theta\}. The choice of prior does not affect the type-I error safety guarantee, hence it is fine, even from a frequentist point of view, if such a prior is chosen based on vague prior knowledge. Still, the prior affects how fast one will tend to reject the null if it is indeed false. For the case that no clear prior knowledge is available, one may use the prior that is optimal in terms of the relative GRO criterion; again the resulting test also has good power properties.

𝙴\mathtt{E}–Variable Perspective; Block-wise Approach; Optional Continuation

In its simplest form, an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable is a nonnegative random variable SS such that under all distributions PP in the null hypothesis,

𝐄P​[S]≤1.{\bf E}_{P}[S]\leq 1. (1.1)

Our test works by first designing 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables for a single block of data, and then later extending these to sequences of blocks Y(1),Y(2),…Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots by multiplication. A block is a set of data consisting of nan_{a} outcomes in group aa and nbn_{b} outcomes in group bb, for some pre-specified nan_{a} and nbn_{b}. The nan_{a} and nbn_{b} used for the jj-th block Y(j)Y_{(j)} are allowed to depend on past data, but they must be fixed before the first observation in block jj occurs (this rule can be loosened to some extent, see Section 2.1).

At each point in time, the running product of block 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables observed so far is itself an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable, and the random process of the products is known as a test martingale. An 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable-based test at level α\alpha is then a test with, in combination with any stopping rule τ\tau, reports ‘reject’ if and only if the product of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-values corresponding to all blocks that were observed so far and have already been completed, is larger than 1/α1/\alpha. The full definition of τ\tau may, and often will, be unknown to the user — the user only needs to get the signal to stop and can then report the product 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable. A classical paired one-sample test corresponds to the special case with na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1 and data coming in in the order a,b,a,b,…a,b,a,b,\ldots.

We can combine 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables from different trials that share a common null (but may be defined relative to a different alternative) by multiplication, and still retain type-I error control. If we used p-values rather than 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables we would have to resort to e.g. Fisher’s method for combining p-values, which, in contrast to multiplication of ee-values, is invalid if there is a dependency between the (decision to perform) tests. With 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables, such dependencies pose no problems for error control. Thus, in our setting, even if the design (i.e. nan_{a} and nbn_{b}) is fixed in advance and optional stopping plays no role, we might still want to use the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable based tests described in this paper rather than a classic p-value based approach, since it allows us to do optional continuation over many experiments/studies (essentially, doing a meta-analysis (Ter Schure et al.,, 2021)) while keeping type-I error control.

𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables and test martingales are explained in more detail in Section 1.1 below, but we refer to Grünwald et al., (2022); Shafer, (2021) for an extensive introduction to 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables, their use in ‘optional continuation’ over several studies, and their enlightening betting interpretation. The general story that emerges from these papers as well as, for example, (Vovk and Wang,, 2021; Ramdas et al.,, 2020) is that 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables and test martingales are the ‘right’ generalization of likelihood ratios to the case that both ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} can be composite and combination of data from several trials may be required.

Relevance

Even in this age of big data and huge models, simple tests for comparing two populations are still used as heavily as ever in clinical trials, psychological studies and so on — areas heavily plagued by the reproducibility crisis (Pace and Salvan,, 2019). In a by-now notorious questionnaire (John et al.,, 2012), more than 55%55\% of the interviewed psychologists admitted to the practice of ‘adding data until the results look good’. While classical methods lose their type-I error guarantee if one does this (Figure S3.1 in Appendix S3 in the Supporting Material), 𝙴\mathtt{E}–value based tests allow for it, while, due to the option of stopping early, remaining competitive in terms of sample sizes needed to obtain a desired power. We illustrate the practical advantage of our test in Section 6 using the recent real-world example of the SWEPIS trial which was stopped early for harm (Wennerholm et al.,, 2019). Their analysis being based on a p-value (by definition designed for fixed sampling plan), the question whether there was indeed sufficient evidence available to stop early is very hard to answer, since the sampling plan was not followed so that the p-value that led them to stop was by definition incorrectly calculated. This also makes it very difficult to combine the test results with results from earlier or future data while keeping anything like error control. We show that with our 𝙴\mathtt{E}–value based methodology we would have obtained sufficient evidence to stop for harm after the same number of events had occurred. Additionally, this 𝙴\mathtt{E}–value, even though based on a stopped trial, can be effortlessly combined with 𝙴\mathtt{E}–values from other trials while retaining error guarantees. Also, our results are of interest beyond mere testing: the 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variables we develop in this paper can be used to obtain anytime-valid confidence intervals (Howard et al.,, 2021) that also remain valid under optional stopping. We will report on this extension elsewhere.

SWEPIS summarized its data as a 2×22\times 2 contingency table. In Section 3 and 4 we refine our generic test to the 2×22\times 2and k×2k\times 2 model. An advantage of focusing on this simple setting is that it is arguably the simplest and clearest example in which there is a nuisance parameter (the proportion under the null) that does not admit a group invariance. Nuisance parameters that satisfy such an invariance (such as the variance in the tt-test, or the grand mean in the two-sample tt-test) are quite straightforward to turn into 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variables and test martingales via the method of maximal invariants, as explained by Grünwald et al., (2022) and already put into practice by e.g. Robbins, (1970); Lai, (1976). The present paper shows that the proportion under the null can also be handled in a clean and simple manner. As explained below, the resulting instantiated 2×22\times 2 test appears to be quite different from existing sequential and Bayesian approaches. Thus, more than 85 years after the lady tasting tea, we are able to still say something quite new about the age-old problem of contingency table testing.

Related Work

A sequential test for the 2×22\times 2 setting has been suggested as early as 1947 by Wald in his seminal (Wald,, 1947) . Wald’s test can be turned into a product of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables and would then be safe to use under optional stopping. Yet, as explained in Section 7.2, in the 2×22\times 2 setting the resulting 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables do not grow as fast as the ones introduced here, and the underlying idea does not generalize to arbitrary models or effect size notions. Other earlier approaches (e.g. (Siegmund,, 2013, Section V.2)) are based on asymptotic approximations. In contrast, our 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable based tests are exact and nonasymptotic. In fact our tests are more closely related to, yet still different from, Bayes factor tests: in the case of simple null hypotheses, 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable based tests coincide with Bayes factors (Grünwald et al.,, 2022). However, in the 2×22\times 2 setting the null is not simple, and while the Bayes factor is a ratio of two Bayes marginal likelihoods, our 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variables are ratios of more general, ‘prequential’ (Dawid,, 1984) likelihood ratios. In some special cases, the numerator is still a Bayes marginal likelihood, but the denominator, in the 2×22\times 2 setting, almost never is (Section 2.2) . Thus, while similar in ‘look’, our approach is in the end quite different from the default Bayes factors for tests of two proportions that were proposed by Kass and Vaidyanathan, (1992) and by Jamil et al., (2017), the latter based on early work by Gunel and Dickey, (1974). To illustrate, in Appendix S2 (Supplementary Material) we show that none of the variants of the Gunel-Dickey Bayes factor that are applicable in our set-up yield valid 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables.

Another, very recent, approach that bears some similarity to ours are the two-sample tests from Manole and Ramdas, (2021). They focus on a nonparametric setting and their test martingales satisfy optimality properties as the sample size gets large. Instead, we focus on the parametric case and, for this case, manage to derive 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables that are equal to or closely approximate the optimal (as measured according to the GRO criterion) 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables, thus optimizing for the small-sample case (in principle, our tests could be used in a nonparametric setting as well, but since they rely on using a prior on the alternative, the test martingales of Manole and Ramdas, (2021) might be easier to use in that case). Another general nonparametric two-sample approach with a sequential flavor (but without optional stopping error guarantees) is Lhéritier and Cazals, (2018).

Contents

In the remainder of this introductory section, we formally introduce 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables, optional stopping and the concept of GRO-optimality. In Section 2 we propose our generic 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for tests of two streams in general and investigate when it has the GRO property. In Sections 3 and 4 we specifically show how these general 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables can be applied in the setting of a test of two proportions, with and without restrictions on the alternative hypothesis. In Sections 5 and 6 we provide, through simulations and a real-world example, comparisons of various 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables and Fisher’s exact test with respect to GRO and power. In Section  7 we compare our generic approach to other 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables one might define for this problem, including the ones based on Wald’s section test. We end with a conclusion. All proofs are in the appendix.

1.1 𝙴\mathtt{E}-Variables and Test Martingales, Safety and Optimality

We first need to extend the notion of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable to random processes:

Definition 1.

Let {Y(j)}j∈𝐍\{Y_{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}}, with all Y(j)Y_{(j)} taking values in some set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, represent a discrete-time random process. Let ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} be a collection of distributions for the process {Y(j)}j∈𝐍\{Y_{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}}. For all j∈𝐍j\in\mathbf{N}, let S(j)S_{(j)} be a non-negative random variable that is adapted to σ⁡(Y(j))\sigma(Y^{(j)}), with Y(j)=(Y(1),…,Y(j))Y^{(j)}=(Y_{(1)},\ldots,Y_{(j)}), i.e. there exists a function ss such that S(j)=s⁡(Y(j))S_{(j)}=s(Y^{(j)}).

  1. 1.

    We say that S(j)S_{(j)} is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable for Y(j)Y_{(j)} conditionally on Y(j−1)Y^{(j-1)} if for all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0},

    𝐄P[S(j)∣Y(1),…,Y(j−1)]≤1.{\bf E}_{P}\left[S_{(j)}\mid Y_{(1)},\ldots,Y_{(j-1)}\right]\leq 1. (1.2)

    That is, for each y(j−1)∈𝒴j−1y^{(j-1)}{}\in\mathcal{Y}^{j-1}, all P0∈ℋ0P_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, (1.1) holds with S=s⁡(y(1),…,y(j−1),Y(j))S=s(y_{(1)},\ldots,y_{(j-1)},Y_{(j)}) and PP set to P0|Y(j−1)=y(j−1)P_{0}\mid Y^{(j-1)}=y^{(j-1)}.

  2. 2.

    If, for each jj, S(j)S_{(j)} is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable conditional on Y(1),…,Y(j−1)Y_{(1)},\ldots,Y_{(j-1)}, then we call the process {S(j)}j∈𝐍\{S_{(j)}{}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}} a sequential 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable process relative to the given ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and {Y(j)}j∈𝐍\{Y_{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}} and we call {S(m)}m∈𝐍\{S^{(m)}{}\}_{m\in\mathbf{N}} with S(m)=∏j=1mS(j)S^{(m)}{}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{(j)} the corresponding test martingale.

Henceforth, we omit the phrase ‘relative to ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and {Y(j)}j∈𝐍\{Y_{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}}’ whenever it is clear from the context. By the tower property of conditional expectation, one verifies that for any process of conditional 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables {S(j)}j∈𝐍\{S_{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}}, we have for all mm that the product S(m)S^{(m)}{} is itself an ‘unconditional’ 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable as in (1.1), i.e. 𝐄P​[S(m)]≤1{\bf E}_{P}[S^{(m)}]\leq 1 for all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}. Definition 1 adapts and slightly modifies terminology from (Shafer et al.,, 2011). As follows from that paper, in standard martingale terminology, what we call a test martingale is a non-negative supermartingale relative to the filtration induced by {Y(j)}j∈𝐍\{Y_{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}}, with starting value 11.

Safety

The interest in 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables and test martingales derives from the fact that we have type-I error control irrespective of the stopping rule used: for any test martingale {S(j)}j∈𝐍\{S^{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}}, Ville’s inequality (Shafer,, 2021) tells us that, for all 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1, P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0},

P⁡(there exists j such that ​S(j)≥1/α)≤α.P(\text{there exists $j$ such that\ }S^{(j)}\geq 1/\alpha)\leq\alpha. (1.3)

Thus, if we measure evidence against the null hypothesis after observing jj data units by S(j)S^{(j)}, and we reject the null hypothesis if S(j)≥1/αS^{(j)}\geq 1/\alpha, then our type-I error will be bounded by α\alpha, no matter what stopping rule we used for determining jj. We thus have type-I error control even if we use the most aggressive stopping rule compatible with this scenario, where we stop at the first jj at which S(j)≥1/αS^{(j)}\geq 1/\alpha (or we run out of data, or money to generate new data). We also have type-I error control if the actual stopping rule is unknown to us, or determined by external factors independent of the data Y(j)Y_{(j)}.

We will call any test based on {S(j)}j∈𝐍\{S^{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}} and a (potentially unknown) stopping time τ\tau that, after stopping, rejects iff S(τ)≥1/αS^{(\tau)}\geq 1/\alpha a level α\alpha-test that is safe under optional stopping, or simply a safe test.

Example 1.

Let P0P_{0} and QQ be any two distributions for the process Y(1),Y(2),…Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots, and let ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} represent a simple null. Let S(m)S^{(m)} denote the likelihood ratio for mm outcomes and S(j)S_{(j)} its constituent factors, i.e.

S(m)=q⁡(Y(m))p0​(Y(m))=∏j=1mS(j)​ with ​S(j)=q⁡(Y(j)∣Y(j−1))p0​(Y(j)∣Y(j−1))S^{(m)}=\frac{q(Y^{(m)})}{p_{0}(Y^{(m)})}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{(j)}\text{\ with\ }S_{(j)}=\frac{q(Y_{(j)}\mid Y^{(j-1)})}{p_{0}(Y_{(j)}\mid Y^{(j-1)})} (1.4)

where q⁡(y(m)∣y(m−1))q(y_{(m)}\mid y^{(m-1)}) denotes the conditional density corresponding to QQ and p0​(y(m)∣y(m−1))p_{0}(y_{(m)}\mid y^{(m-1)}) the one corresponding to P0P_{0} with respect to a common underlying measure. Then the likelihood ratio process {S(m)}m∈𝐍\{S^{(m)}\}_{m\in\mathbf{N}} constitutes a test martingale, and the process of past-conditional likelihoods {S(j)}\{S_{(j)}\} is a sequential 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable process relative to ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. This can be immediately verified by directly calculating the conditional expectation of S(j)S_{(j)} given Y(j−1)Y^{(j-1)}, noticing that the densities p0​(Y(j)|Y(j−1))p_{0}(Y_{(j)}|Y^{(j-1)}) cancel in the calculation.

GRO-Optimality, Simple ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}

Just like for p-values, the definition of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables only requires explicit specification of ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, not of an alternative hypothesis ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} becomes crucial once we distinguish between ‘good’ and ‘bad’ 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables: 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables have been designed to remain small, with high probability, under the null ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. But if ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} rather than ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is true, then ‘good’ 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables should produce evidence (grow — because the larger the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable, the closer we are to rejecting the null) against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} as fast as possible. To make this precise, first consider simple (singleton) ℋ1={Q}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{Q\}. We start with the one-outcome setting of (1.1), i.e. we look at a single 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable S(j)S_{(j)} in isolation for a single outcome Y(j)Y_{(j)}. Its optimality is measured in terms of

𝐄Q​[log⁡S(j)],{\bf E}_{Q}[\log S_{(j)}], (1.5)

and the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable which maximizes this quantity among all 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables that can be written as functions of Y(j)Y_{(j)} (i.e. non-negative random variables satisfying (1.1)), assuming it exists, is called the Growth Rate Optimal 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Y(j)Y_{(j)} relative to QQ, or simply ‘QQ-GRO for Y(j)Y_{(j)}’, and denoted as Sgro​(Q),(j)S_{\text{\sc gro}(Q),(j)} More generally, 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable S(m)S^{(m)} is called growth rate optimal relative to QQ for Y(m)Y^{(m)}, or simply QQ-GRO for Y(m)Y^{(m)}, if, among all (unconditional) 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variables that can be written as a function of Y(m)Y^{(m)}, it maximizes

𝐄Q​[log⁡S(m)].{\bf E}_{Q}[\log S^{(m)}]. (1.6)

We will denote this 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable, if it exists, by Sgro​(Q)(m)S^{(m)}_{\text{\sc gro}(Q)}. The idea to maximize (1.6) goes back to Kelly, (1956); the GRO-terminology is from Grünwald et al., (2022). The larger an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable or test martingale tends to be under the alternative, the better it scores in the GRO sense. Of course, the same would still hold if we were to replace the logarithm by another strictly increasing function. But there are various compelling reasons for why one should take a logarithm here — see Grünwald et al., (2022); Shafer, (2021). One interesting reason, not explicitly covered by these two papers, was already given by Breiman, (1961) and is explained in detail by (Ter Schure et al.,, 2021, Appendix B.1): the QQ-GRO test martingale is also the test martingale which minimizes the expected number of data points needed before the null can be rejected if we use the test with the aggressive stopping rule described before (reject at the smallest jj such that OPENS(j)≥1/α)S^{(j)}\geq 1/\alpha). Thus, using the QQ-GRO test martingale is quite analogous to employing a test that maximizes power. One can also directly see that both notions must be connected by noting that GRO implies optimizing the expectation of log⁡S(j)\log S^{(j)} whereas power at fixed sample size jj is the probability that log⁡S(j)\log S^{(j)} is larger than −log⁡α-\log\alpha. Note that we cannot directly use power in designing tests, since the notion of power requires a fixed sampling plan, which we will usually not have: we may not want or not be able to stop at the first jj such that we can reject — for example, we might want to stop early for harm (Section 6), or we might want to lower α\alpha if the first few outcomes look very promising. So we will measure optimality in terms of GRO instead, but for practical usefulness we do hope that, in cases where we do follow the sampling plan above (stop as soon as OPENS(j)≥1/α)S^{(j)}\geq 1/\alpha)), our power remains reasonable. This is suggested by Breiman’s observation above, but we want to check it nevertheless. Such a check is done successfully for the 2×22\times 2 model in Section 5.

In ‘nice’ cases, the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable (1.6) for mm outcomes can be obtained by multiplying the individual QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variables:

Proposition 1.

Let ℋ1={Q}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{Q\} be simple and ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} be potentially composite, and ‘nondegenerate’ in the sense that for some P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, D(Q∥P)<∞D(Q\|P)<\infty, D(⋅∥⋅)D(\cdot\|\cdot) denoting the KL divergence. Suppose the following condition holds (with qq, pp the density of QQ and PP, respectively):

There exists a P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0} such that S(1)=q⁡(Y(1))/p⁡(Y(1))S_{(1)}=q(Y_{(1)})/p(Y_{(1)}) is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable. (1.7)

Then S(1)=Sgro​(Q),(1)S_{(1)}=S_{\text{\sc gro}(Q),(1)} is the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Y(1)Y_{(1)}. An 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable of this form automatically exists if ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is simple. If we further assume that Y(1),Y(2),…Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots are i.i.d. according to all distributions in ℋ0∪ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{0}\cup\mathcal{H}_{1}, then Sgro​(Q)(m)=∏j=1mSgro​(Q),(j)S^{(m)}_{\text{\sc gro}(Q)}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{\text{\sc gro}(Q),(j)}, i.e. the QQ-GRO optimal (unconditional) 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Y(m)Y^{(m)} is the product of the individual QQ-GRO optimal 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables.

If Condition (1.7) holds and Y(1),Y(2),…Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots are i.i.d. according to all distributions in ℋ0∪ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{0}\cup\mathcal{H}_{1}, it thus makes sense to define the QQ-GRO test martingale to be the test martingale (Sgro​(Q)(j))j∈𝐍(S^{(j)}_{\text{\sc gro}(Q)})_{j\in\mathbf{N}}. We will then have that Sgro​(Q),(j)=sQ​(Y(j))S_{\text{\sc gro}(Q),(j)}=s_{Q}(Y_{(j)}) for a fixed function sQ:𝒴→𝐑0+s_{Q}:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbf{R}^{+}_{0}.

Example 2.

[Simple ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and Simple ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}] Consider ℋ1={Q}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{Q\} and simple ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} and arbitrary Q′Q^{\prime} such that the Y(j)Y_{(j)} are i.i.d. according to P,QP,Q and Q′Q^{\prime}. By the Proposition above, the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Y(j)Y_{(j)} is given by setting q′=qq^{\prime}=q. Then 𝐄Q​[Sgro​(Q),(j)]=𝐄Y(j)∼Q​[log⁡q⁡(Y(j))/p0​(Y(j))]{\bf E}_{Q}[S_{\text{\sc gro}(Q),(j)}]={\bf E}_{Y_{(j)}\sim Q}[\log q(Y_{(j)})/p_{0}(Y_{(j)})] also coincides with the KL divergence between QQ and P0P_{0}.

In Section 2 (Theorem 1) we develop functions sQs_{Q} (denoted s⁡(⋅,na,nb,θa∗,θb∗)s(\cdot;n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}) there) for simple ℋ1={Q}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{Q\} so that SQ,(1)=sQ​(Y(1))S_{Q,(1)}=s_{Q}(Y_{(1)}) is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable even though ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is composite and not convex, so that Proposition 1 does not apply. Since we invariably assume the Y(j)Y_{(j)} are i.i.d., SQ,(j):=sQ​(Y(j))S_{Q,(j)}:=s_{Q}(Y_{(j)}) is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable as well and with SQ(m):=∏j=1mSQ,(j)S^{(m)}_{Q}:=\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{Q,(j)}, (SQ(m))m∈𝐍(S^{(m)}_{Q})_{m\in\mathbf{N}} is a test martingale. The construction works for the general setting of two data streams discussed in the introduction, and for some special ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} (even though composite and nonconvex), the SQ,(j)S_{Q,(j)} will in fact be QQ-GRO and (SQ(m))m∈𝐍(S^{(m)}_{Q})_{m\in\mathbf{N}} will be the QQ-GRO test martingale. These include the ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} that arise in the 2×22\times 2 setting, our main application. For other ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, the 𝙴−\mathtt{E}- variables SQ,(j)S_{Q,(j)} will not necessarily have the QQ-GRO-property; they are designed to have (1.6) large, but it may be even larger for other 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables.

GRO and Composite ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}

In case ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is composite, no direct analogue of the GRO-criterion for designing 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables exists, since it is not clear under what distribution Q∈ℋ1Q\in\mathcal{H}_{1} we should maximize (1.6). In this paper, we deal with this situation by learning QQ from the data in a Bayesian fashion. It is now convenient to write ℋ1={Pθ:θ∈Θ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{1}\} in a parameterized manner (accordingly, henceforth we shall write θ1\theta_{1}-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable instead of Pθ1P_{\theta_{1}}-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable and Sgro​(θ),(j)S_{\text{\sc gro}(\theta),(j)} instead of Sgro​(Pθ),(j)S_{\text{\sc gro}(P_{\theta}),(j)}). We will assume i.i.d. data, thus, if ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} were true, then data would be i.i.d. ∼Pθ1∗\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{1}} for some θ1∗∈Θ1\theta^{*}_{1}\in\Theta_{1}. Starting with a distribution WW on Θ1\Theta_{1}, i.e. a prior, at each point in time jj, we determine the Bayesian posterior W|Y(j−1)W\mid Y^{(j-1)} and use the Bayes predictive PW|Y(j−1):=∫Θ1Pθ​𝑑W​(θ∣Y(j−1))P_{W\mid Y^{(j-1)}}:=\int_{\Theta_{1}}P_{\theta}dW(\theta\mid Y^{(j-1)}) as an estimate for the ‘true’ Pθ1∗P_{\theta^{*}_{1}}. As is well-known, under conditions on WW and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} (which, if ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is finite-dimensional parametric, are very mild), the posterior will concentrate around θ∗{\theta^{*}} and hence PW|Y(j−1)P_{W\mid Y^{(j-1)}} will resemble Pθ1∗P_{\theta^{*}_{1}} more and more, with very high probability, as more data becomes available.

At each point in time jj, we use our current estimate PW|Y(j−1)P_{W\mid Y^{(j-1)}} to design a conditional 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable S(j)S_{(j)}. On an informal level, as long as PW|Y(j−1)P_{W\mid Y^{(j-1)}} converges to the ‘true’ Pθ1∗P_{\theta^{*}_{1}}, the S(j)S_{(j)} will in fact also start to more and more resemble the 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variables Sgro​(θ1∗),(j)S_{\text{\sc gro}(\theta^{*}_{1}),(j)} we designed for ℋ1={Pθ1∗}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta^{*}_{1}}\} and which were designed to have a large expected growth under the ‘true’ Pθ1∗P_{\theta^{*}_{1}}. Assuming the convergence happens fast, we have that

𝐄Y(m)∼Pθ1∗[logSgro​(θ1∗)(m)−log∏j=1mS(j)]\displaystyle{\bf E}_{Y^{(m)}\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{1}}}\left[\log S^{(m)}_{\text{\sc gro}(\theta^{*}_{1})}-\log\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{(j)}\right] (1.8)

is small, i.e. we may expect that the test martingale ∏j=1mS(j)\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{(j)} grows not much slower than Sgro​(θ1∗)(m)=∏j=1mSgro​(θ1∗),(j)S^{(m)}_{\text{\sc gro}(\theta^{*}_{1})}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{\text{\sc gro}(\theta^{*}_{1}),(j)}, the best test martingale (maximizing 𝐄Y(m)∼Pθ1∗​[log⁡S]{\bf E}_{Y^{(m)}\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{1}}}\left[\log S\right] over all 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables SS for Y(m)Y^{(m)}) we could have used if we had known the true Pθ1∗P_{\theta^{*}_{1}} all along.

2 Two-Stream Safe Tests

Consider the two-stream setting introduced in the beginning of the paper. To formalize it further, we introduce calendar time t=1,2,…t=1,2,\ldots and corresponding random variables VtV_{t} and GtG_{t}: at each tt, we obtain an outcome VtV_{t} in 𝒴\mathcal{Y} in group Gt∈{a,b}G_{t}\in\{a,b\}. Importantly though, at this point we make no assumptions about the relative ordering of outcomes from the two groups. At time tt, we have that tat_{a}, the number of aa’s that are observed so far, and tbt_{b}, the number of bb’s observed so far, satisfy ta+tb=tt_{a}+t_{b}=t, but subject to this constraint we allow them coming in any order, e.g. first all aa’s, or first all bb’s, or interleaved. For example, with ta=3t_{a}=3 and tb=2t_{b}=2, we might have V1=Y1,a,V2=Y2,a,V3=Y3,a,V4=Y1,b,V5=Y2,bV_{1}=Y_{1,a},V_{2}=Y_{2,a},V_{3}=Y_{3,a},V_{4}=Y_{1,b},V_{5}=Y_{2,b} (all aas come first, G1=G2=G3=a,G4=G5=bG_{1}=G_{2}=G_{3}=a,G_{4}=G_{5}=b) but also, for example V1=Y1,a,V2=Y1,b,V3=Y2,a,V4=Y3,a,V5=Y2,bV_{1}=Y_{1,a},V_{2}=Y_{1,b},V_{3}=Y_{2,a},V_{4}=Y_{3,a},V_{5}=Y_{2,b}.

We thus have that the (marginal) probability of the first t=ta+tbt=t_{a}+t_{b} outcomes, given that tat_{a} of these are in group aa and tbt_{b} in group bb, and writing yt=(y1,…,yt)y^{t}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{t}), is given by the probability density (or mass function)

pθa,θb​(yata,ybtb)≔pθa​(yata)​pθb​(ybtb)=∏t=1tapθa​(yt,a)​∏t=1tbpθb​(yt,b).p_{\theta_{a},\theta_{b}}(y_{a}^{t_{a}},y^{t_{b}}_{b})\coloneqq p_{\theta_{a}}(y_{a}^{t_{a}})p_{\theta_{b}}(y^{t_{b}}_{b})=\prod_{t=1}^{t_{a}}p_{\theta_{a}}(y_{t,a})\prod_{t=1}^{t_{b}}p_{\theta_{b}}(y_{t,b}). (2.1)

To indicate that random vector (Yata,Ybtb)≔(Y1,a​…,Yta,a,Y1,b,…,Ytb,b)(Y^{t_{a}}_{a},Y^{t_{b}}_{b})\coloneqq(Y_{1,a}\ldots,Y_{t_{a},a},Y_{1,b},\ldots,Y_{t_{b},b}) has a distribution represented by (2.1) we write ‘Yata,Ybtb∼Pθa∗,θb∗Y^{t_{a}}_{a},Y^{t_{b}}_{b}\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}}’.

According to the null hypothesis ℋ0={Pθa,θb:(θa,θb)∈Θ0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\theta_{a},\theta_{b}}:(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})\in\Theta_{0}\}, Θ0={(θ,θ):θ∈Θ}\Theta_{0}=\{(\theta,\theta):\theta\in\Theta\}, both processes coincide. Thus, we have that θa∗=θb∗=θ0\theta^{*}_{a}=\theta^{*}_{b}=\theta_{0} for some θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\Theta and then the density of data yata,ybtby_{a}^{t_{a}},y^{t_{b}}_{b} is given by pθ0​(y1,a,…,yta,a,y1,b,…,ytb,b)p_{\theta_{0}}(y_{1,a},\ldots,y_{t_{a},a},y_{1,b},\ldots,y_{t_{b},b}).

2.1 A generic 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for 2-stream–blocks

We first consider the case in which the alternative hypothesis is simple: Θ1={θ1}\Theta_{1}=\{\theta_{1}\} for some fixed θ1=(θa∗,θb∗)∈Θ2\theta_{1}=(\theta_{a}^{*},\theta_{b}^{*})\in\Theta^{2}. Consider a fixed sample size of size nn, and assume that we will observe a block of nan_{a} outcomes in group aa and nbn_{b} outcomes in group bb. In this case, we can define an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable as the likelihood ratio between pθa∗,θb∗p_{\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}} and a carefully chosen distribution that is a product of mixtures of distributions from Θ0\Theta_{0}: for na,nb∈𝐍n_{a},n_{b}\in\mathbf{N}, n≔na+nbn\coloneqq n_{a}+n_{b} and yana=(y1,a,…,yna,a)∈𝒴nay^{n_{a}}_{a}=(y_{1,a},\ldots,y_{n_{a},a})\in\mathcal{Y}^{n_{a}} and ybnb=(y1,b,…,ynb,b)∈𝒴nby^{n_{b}}_{b}=(y_{1,b},\ldots,y_{n_{b},b})\in\mathcal{Y}^{n_{b}}, we define:

s⁡(yana,ybnb,na,nb,θa∗,θb∗)≔pθa∗​(yana)∏i=1na(nan​pθa∗​(yi,a)+nbn​pθb∗​(yi,a))⋅pθb∗​(ybnb)∏i=1nb(nan​pθa∗​(yi,b)+nbn​pθb∗​(yi,b)).s(y^{n_{a}}_{a},y^{n_{b}}_{b};n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b})\coloneqq\\ \frac{p_{\theta_{a}^{*}}(y^{n_{a}}_{a})}{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{a}}\left(\frac{n_{a}}{n}p_{\theta^{*}_{a}}(y_{i,a})+\frac{n_{b}}{n}p_{\theta^{*}_{b}}(y_{i,a})\right)}\cdot\frac{p_{\theta_{b}^{*}}(y^{n_{b}}_{b})}{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{b}}\left(\frac{n_{a}}{n}p_{\theta^{*}_{a}}(y_{i,b})+\frac{n_{b}}{n}p_{\theta^{*}_{b}}(y_{i,b})\right)}. (2.2)
Theorem 1.

The random variable S[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗]:=s⁡(Yana,Ybnb,na,nb,θa∗,θb∗)S_{[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]}:=s(Y^{n_{a}}_{a},Y^{n_{b}}_{b};n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}) is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable, i.e. we have:

supθ∈Θ𝐄Vn∼Pθ​[s⁡(Vn,na,nb,θa∗,θb∗)]≤1.\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}{\bf E}_{V^{n}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[s(V^{n};n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b})\right]\leq 1.

Moreover, if {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} is a convex set of distributions, then S[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗]S_{[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]} is the (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b})-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable: for any non-negative function s′s^{\prime} on 𝒴na+nb\mathcal{Y}^{n_{a}+n_{b}} satisfying supθ∈Θ𝐄Vn∼Pθ​[s′​(Vn)]≤1\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}{\bf E}_{V^{n}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[s^{\prime}(V^{n})\right]\leq 1, we have:

𝐄Yana,Ybnb∼Pθa∗,θb∗​[log⁡s⁡(Yana,Ybnb,na,nb,θa∗,θb∗)]≥𝐄Yana,Ybnb∼Pθa∗,θb∗​[log⁡s′​(Yana,Ybnb)].{\bf E}_{Y^{n_{a}}_{a},Y^{n_{b}}_{b}\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}}}[\log s(Y^{n_{a}}_{a},Y^{n_{b}}_{b};n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b})]\geq{\bf E}_{Y^{n_{a}}_{a},Y^{n_{b}}_{b}\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}}}[\log s^{\prime}(Y^{n_{a}}_{a},Y^{n_{b}}_{b})].

Crucially, in the second part of the theorem, we do not require convexity of ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, a set of distributions over 𝒴na+nb\mathcal{Y}^{n_{a}+n_{b}} (if ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} were convex, the GRO property would already follow automatically (Koolen and Grünwald,, 2021)), but instead of {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}, a set of distributions on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. In the 2×22\times 2 case ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is not convex, since the set of i.i.d. Bernoulli distributions over na+nb>1n_{a}+n_{b}>1 outcomes is not convex; but {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} is just the Bernoulli model on one outcome, which is convex, so that in this setting, we get the GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable.

To illustrate, consider the basic case in which data comes in in fixed batches Y(1),Y(2),…Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots, with each batch Y(j)=((Y(j−1)​na+1,a,Y(j−1)​na+2,a,…,Yj​na,a)CLOSEY_{(j)}=((Y_{(j-1)n_{a}+1,a},Y_{(j-1)n_{a}+2,a},\ldots,Y_{jn_{a},a}) ,(Y(j−1)​nb+1,b,Y(j−1)​nb+2,b,…,Yj​nb,b)),,(Y_{(j-1)n_{b}+1,b},Y_{(j-1)n_{b}+2,b},\ldots,Y_{jn_{b},b})), having exactly nan_{a} outcomes in group aa and nbn_{b} outcomes in group bb, and let n=na+nbn=n_{a}+n_{b}. This case would obtain, for example, in a sequential clinical trial in which patients come in one by one, each odd patient is given the treatment and each even patient is given the placebo. Then n=2n=2, na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1. We may then measure the evidence against the null hypothesis by the product E-value

S[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗](m)≔∏j=1mS(j),[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗];S(j),[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗]≔s⁡(Y(j),na,nb,θa∗,θb∗).S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]}\coloneqq\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{(j),[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]}\ \ ;\ \ S_{(j),[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]}\coloneqq s(Y_{(j)};n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}). (2.3)

By Ville’s inequality (1.3), the probability under any distribution in the null that there is an mm with S[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗](m)S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]} larger than 1/α1/\alpha, is bounded by α\alpha, hence, type-I error guarantees are preserved under optional stopping if we perform the test based on {S[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗](m)}m∈𝐍\{S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]}\}_{m\in\mathbf{N}} as defined underneath (1.3), as long as we stop between and not ‘within’ batches (if we stop within a batch, the E-variable S[na,nb,θa∗,θb∗](m)S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}]} is undefined).

If the data do not come in batches of equal size, we may proceed as follows. First, we need to fix some na≥1n_{a}\geq 1 and nb≥1n_{b}\geq 1 of our own choice. The treatment below will give valid 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables irrespective of our choice of nan_{a} and nbn_{b}, but it will be seen that some choices are much more reasonable (will lead to much more evidence against the null, if the null is false) than others.

Thus, fix nan_{a} and nbn_{b}, set n=na+nbn=n_{a}+n_{b}. At each time tt, we will have observed, so far, some number tat_{a} of outcomes in group aa, and tbt_{b} in group bb. Now let mtm_{t} be the largest mm such that m​na≤tamn_{a}\leq t_{a} and m​nb≤tbmn_{b}\leq t_{b}. Now, for m=1,2,…m=1,2,\ldots, define Y(m)Y_{(m)} as above. At any given time tt, Y(1),Y(2),…,Y(mt)Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots,Y_{(m_{t})} will have been observed, and there may be a number nj′n^{\prime}_{j} remaining observations in group j∈{a,b}j\in\{a,b\} so that either na′<nan^{\prime}_{a}<n_{a} or nb′<nbn^{\prime}_{b}<n_{b} or both. Since the {Y(j)}j∈𝐍\{Y_{(j)}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}} determine a test martingale in the sense of Definition 1, optional stopping while preserving type-I error guarantees is then possible at any point in time tt, as long as the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable is calculated as (2.3) above for m=mtm=m_{t}, thus ignoring the final na′+nb′n^{\prime}_{a}+n^{\prime}_{b} outcomes.

How should nan_{a} and nbn_{b} be chosen in practice? For example, consider a variation of the clinical trial setting above in which the treatment-control assignment is randomized: for each incoming patient, a fair coin is flipped to decide treatment (a)(a) or placebo (b)(b). Then at any given time the number of patients in group aa and bb will not be precisely equal, but if we choose na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1 as above it is highly unlikely that the amount of data we have to ignore at any given time tt is very large. Similarly, if GtG_{t}, the group membership of the tt-th observation is itself i.i.d. according to some distribution P∗P^{*}, we might have some idea of the probability p∗​(a)p^{*}(a) assigned to group aa; if p∗​(a)=2/5p^{*}(a)=2/5 (say), we would choose na=2,nb=3n_{a}=2,n_{b}=3.

We can add a significant amount of extra flexibility by allowing for variable group sizes, i.e., the chosen nan_{a} and nbn_{b} may depend on the past. For this, we introduce a function f:⋃t≥0𝒴t×{0,1}t→{stop-block,continue}f:\bigcup_{t\geq 0}\mathcal{Y}^{t}\times\{0,1\}^{t}\rightarrow\{\text{\sc stop-block},\text{\sc continue}\} that, at each point in time tt, decides whether the current block should end (f⁡(Vt,Gt)=stop-block)(f(V^{t},G^{t})=\text{\sc stop-block}) or not (f⁡(Vt,Gt)=continue)(f(V^{t},G^{t})=\text{\sc continue}). As long as the value of this function does not depend on the actual outcomes VtV_{t} observed after the last block that was completed, all requirements for having a test martingale and thus for safe optional stopping are met. For example, suppose that on data V1,G1,V2,G2,…,Vt,GtV_{1},G_{1},V_{2},G_{2},\ldots,V_{t},G_{t} observed so-far, ff has output stop-block at mm occasions, the last time at t′=t−kt^{\prime}=t-k for some k>0k>0. Then f⁡(t)f(t) is allowed to depend on Y(m)Y^{(m)} and GtG^{t}, but for any fixed Y(m)=y(m),Gt=gtY^{(m)}=y^{(m)},G^{t}=g^{t}, for all yk,y′k∈𝒴ky^{k},y^{\prime k}\in\mathcal{Y}^{k}, we must have f⁡((y(m),yk),gt)=f⁡((y(m),y′k),gt)f((y^{(m)},y^{k}),g^{t})=f((y^{(m)},y^{\prime k}),g^{t}). In this way, one can in principle learn p∗​(a)p^{*}(a) from the data, changing group sizes nan_{a} and nbn_{b} flexibly as data come in. For simplicity, we have not followed this approach here, but all our results readily extend to this case.

Extension to kk-sample streams

It is entirely straightforward to extend (2.2) to the scenario where we do not compare 22, but kk i.i.d. data streams. Indeed, in the appendix we state and prove the generalization of Theorem 1 to kk data streams. We again consider some fixed θ→=(θa,θb,…,θk)∈Θk\vec{\theta}=(\theta_{a},\theta_{b},...,\theta_{k})\in\Theta^{k}. The probability of the first t=∑g=1ktgt=\sum_{g=1}^{k}t_{g} outcomes is now given by the density or mass function pθ→≔pθa​(yata)​pθa​(ybtb)​…​pθk​(yktk)p_{\vec{\theta}}\coloneqq p_{\theta_{a}}(y_{a}^{t_{a}})p_{\theta_{a}}(y_{b}^{t_{b}})...p_{\theta_{k}}(y_{k}^{t_{k}}). We now need to fix the kk group outcome numbers n→≔(na,nb,…,nk)\vec{n}\coloneqq(n_{a},n_{b},...,n_{k}) in advance, which allows us to define the extended 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable as a function of the data y→n=(yana,ybnb,…,yknk)\vec{y}^{n}=(y_{a}^{n_{a}},y_{b}^{n_{b}},...,y_{k}^{n_{k}}), with n=∑g=1kngn=\sum_{g=1}^{k}n_{g}:

s⁡(y→n,n→,θ→∗)≔∏g=1kpθg∗​(ygng)∏i=1ng(∑g′=1kng′n​pθg′∗​(yi,g)),s(\vec{y}^{n};\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*})\coloneqq\prod_{g=1}^{k}\frac{p_{\theta_{g}^{*}}(y^{n_{g}}_{g})}{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{g}}\left(\sum_{g^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{n_{g^{\prime}}}{n}p_{\theta^{*}_{g^{\prime}}}(y_{i,g})\right)}, (2.4)

for testing the null where θa=θb=…=θk\theta_{a}=\theta_{b}=...=\theta_{k}; it is again GRO if {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} is convex. We now return to the notationally simpler 2-sample case except for a short example of an application of this extension as a flexible and exact alternative to the chi-square test in section 5.

2.2 The generic 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable with Bayesian alternative

Now fix some prior W1W_{1} with density w1w_{1} on the alternative Θ1⊆Θ2\Theta_{1}\subseteq\Theta^{2}. We can trivially extend the definition of our generic 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable relative to singleton (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}) to an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable relative to arbitrary prior W1W_{1} on (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}): define pW1,a​(y):=∫pθa​(y)​d​W1​(θa)p_{W_{1},a}(y):=\int p_{\theta_{a}}(y)dW_{1}(\theta_{a}), the integration being over the marginal prior distribution over θa\theta_{a}, and similarly, pW1,b​(y):=∫pθb​(y)​d​W1​(θb)p_{W_{1},b}(y):=\int p_{\theta_{b}}(y)dW_{1}(\theta_{b}). Then, as a corollary of Theorem 1,

s⁡(yana,ybnb,na,nb,W1)≔∏i=1napW1,a​(yi,a)∏i=1na(nan​pW1,a​(yi,a)+nbn​pW1,b​(yi,a))⋅∏i=1nbpW1,b​(yi,b)∏i=1nb(nan​pW1,a​(yi,b)+nbn​pW1,b​(yi,b)).s(y^{n_{a}}_{a},y^{n_{b}}_{b};n_{a},n_{b},W_{1})\coloneqq\\ \frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{a}}p_{W_{1,a}}(y_{i,a})}{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{a}}\left(\frac{n_{a}}{n}p_{W_{1,a}}(y_{i,a})+\frac{n_{b}}{n}p_{W_{1,b}}(y_{i,a})\right)}\cdot\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{b}}p_{W_{1,b}}(y_{i,b})}{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{b}}\left(\frac{n_{a}}{n}p_{W_{1,a}}(y_{i,b})+\frac{n_{b}}{n}p_{W_{1,b}}(y_{i,b})\right)}. (2.5)

is itself also an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable, as follows from applying Theorem 1 with a ‘meta’-set of distributions, which is possible since we made no assumptions at all on the set Θ\Theta in Theorem 1: we replace Θ\Theta by 𝒲⁡(Θ)\mathcal{W}(\Theta), the set of distributions on Θ\Theta; we replace the background set of distributions {pθ:θ∈Θ}\{p_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} by the set of distributions {pW:W∈𝒲⁡(Θ)}\{p_{W}:W\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta)\}; we replace the simple ℋ1={Pθa∗,θb∗}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}}\} by a ‘simple’ ℋ1′={PWa,Wb}\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{1}=\{P_{W_{a},W_{b}}\} for some distributions WaW_{a} and WbW_{b} on Θ\Theta. Thus, assume again that data comes in batches Y(1),Y(2),…Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots with each Y(j)Y_{(j)} consisting of nan_{a} outcomes in group aa and nbn_{b} outcomes in group bb (generalization to flexible group sizes changing in time and depending on the past as described at the end of Section 2.1 is straightforward). We start with some prior W1W_{1} for the first batch Y(1)Y_{(1)} but we now use, for the jj-th batch Y(j)Y_{(j)}, the Bayesian posterior W1|Y(j−1)W_{1}\mid Y^{(j-1)} as prior to define the jj-th 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable with:

S[na,nb,W1](m)≔∏j=1mS(j),[na,nb,W1];S(j),[na,nb,W1]≔s⁡(Y(j);na,nb,W1|Y(j−1)).S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W_{1}]}\coloneqq\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{(j),[n_{a},n_{b},W_{1}]}\ \ ;\ \ S_{(j),[n_{a},n_{b},W_{1}]}\coloneqq s(Y_{(j)};n_{a},n_{b},W_{1}|Y^{(j-1)}). (2.6)

Again, {S(j),[na,nb,W1]}j∈𝐍\{S_{(j),[n_{a},n_{b},W_{1}]}\}_{j\in\mathbf{N}} is a sequential 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable process, so testing based on the corresponding test martingale is safe under optional stopping by (1.3). If data are sampled from some alternative hypothesis (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}), then as data accumulates, the posterior W1W_{1} will, with high probability, concentrate narrowly around (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}) and so S(j),[na,nb,W1]S_{(j),[n_{a},n_{b},W_{1}]} will behave more and more similarly to the ‘best’ (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta_{a}^{*},\theta_{b}^{*}) 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable. Still, with the exception of a special case we indicate below, in general we cannot expect it to be the W1W_{1}-GRO E-variable. But we are not particularly concerned by this: our experiments in Section 5 indicate that, at least in the 2×22\times 2 table setting, it behaves quite well in terms of power, which is often the main practical interest.

Connection to Bayes Factors

Consider W1W_{1} such that θa\theta_{a} and θb\theta_{b} are independent under W1W_{1} with marginal distributions WaW_{a} and WbW_{b}, and now further take na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1. By basic telescoping, and using that, if independent under the prior, θa\theta_{a} and θb\theta_{b} must also be independent under the posterior, we can then further rewrite (2.6) as

∫pθa​(Yam)​d​Wa​(θa)​∫pθb​(Ybm)​d​Wb​(θb)∏j=1m∏g∈{a,b}(12​pW1,a|Y(j−1)​(Yj,g)+12​pW1,b|Y(j−1)​(Yj,g))=if {Pθ:θ∈Θ} convex\displaystyle\frac{\int p_{\theta_{a}}(Y^{m}_{a})dW_{a}(\theta_{a})\int p_{\theta_{b}}(Y^{m}_{b})dW_{b}(\theta_{b})}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}\prod_{g\in\{a,b\}}\left(\frac{1}{2}p_{W_{1,a}|Y^{(j-1)}}(Y_{j,g})+\frac{1}{2}p_{W_{1,b}|Y^{(j-1)}}(Y_{j,g})\right)}\ \overset{\text{if $\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}$ convex}}{=} (2.8)
∫pθa​(Yam)​d​Wa​(θa)​∫pθb​(Ybm)​d​Wb​(θb)∏j=1m∏g∈{a,b}pθ˘0|Y(j−1)​(Yj,g)\displaystyle\frac{\int p_{\theta_{a}}(Y^{m}_{a})dW_{a}(\theta_{a})\int p_{\theta_{b}}(Y^{m}_{b})dW_{b}(\theta_{b})}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}\prod_{g\in\{a,b\}}p_{\breve{\theta}_{0}|Y^{(j-1)}}(Y_{j,g})} (2.9)

where the equality holds if {Pθ:θ∈Θ0}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{0}\} is convex and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is finite so that (2.7) holds. As seen from (2.8), even without finiteness or convexity, the numerator of the generic product 𝙴\mathtt{E}–value is now equal to the Bayesian marginal likelihood of the data based on prior W1W_{1}. Thus, in this special case (i.e. na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1, prior independence; the derivation breaks down if these do not hold), if the denominator could also be written as a Bayes marginal likelihood, then our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable would really be a Bayes factor. Yet, even if {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} is convex, it cannot be written in this way, though it is very ‘close’: each of the mm factors in the denominator in (2.9) is the product density function of two identical distributions for one outcome, and Proposition 2 shows that, in the special case of the 2×22\times 2 model with WaW_{a} and WbW_{b} independent beta priors, this distribution may itself be the Bayes predictive distribution obtained by equipping Θ0\Theta_{0} with another beta prior. Still, for a real Bayes factor corresponding to ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, for each jj, the two outcomes Yj,a,Yj,bY_{j,a},Y_{j,b} in the jj-th block would not be independent given Y(j−1)Y^{(j-1)}, whereas in (2.9) they are, so we may conclude that in general, our e-variables are not equivalent to any Bayes factor.

Simplified Calculations with Independent Beta Priors

Now take the special case in which θa\theta_{a} and θb\theta_{b} are independent under the prior W1W_{1} with marginals WaW_{a} and WbW_{b}. In this case, θa\theta_{a} and θb\theta_{b} are also independent under the posterior, and we can simplify θ˘a|Y(j−1)=𝐄θa∼Wa|Ya(j−1)​na​[θa]\breve{\theta}_{a}|Y^{(j-1)}={\bf E}_{\theta_{a}\sim W_{a}\mid Y^{(j-1)n_{a}}_{a}}[\theta_{a}], the expectation of θa\theta_{a} under the posterior WaW_{a} given all data so far in group aa, and similarly for group bb. Using beta priors, this expectation is easy to calculate and we get:

Proposition 2.

Let θa,θb\theta_{a},\theta_{b} be independent under W1W_{1}, with marginals WaW_{a} and WbW_{b} respectively. Suppose that these are beta priors with parameters (αa,βa)(\alpha_{a},\beta_{a}) and (αb,βb)(\alpha_{b},\beta_{b}) respectively.
