In the special case that we fix the prior parameters in the groups proportional to the group size fraction κ:=nb/na\kappa:=n_{b}/n_{a}, i.e we fix αb=κ​αa\alpha_{b}=\kappa\alpha_{a}, βb=κ​βa\beta_{b}=\kappa\beta_{a}, the expression for θ˘0\breve{\theta}_{0} simplifies to θ˘0|Y(j−1)=(U+(1+κ)​αa)/((j−1)​n+(1+κ)​αa+(1+κ)​βa)\breve{\theta}_{0}|Y^{(j-1)}=(U+(1+\kappa)\alpha_{a})/((j-1)n+(1+\kappa)\alpha_{a}+(1+\kappa)\beta_{a}).

4 (Un)Restricted Composite ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} in the 2×22\times 2 setting

In this section we describe the main instantiations of the 2×22\times 2 stream testing scenario that are relevant in practice. These differ in the choice of ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}: the choice can be fully unrestricted (we simply want to find whether there is any discrepancy from ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} at all); restricted in terms of effect size; or restricted because we have prior knowledge about either θa∗\theta^{*}_{a} or θb∗\theta^{*}_{b}. We consider each in turn, the second and third scenario in a separate subsection. Section 5 provides extensive numerical simulations for all three scenarios.

In the first scenario, a researcher wants to perform a two-sided test; they simply aim to find any discrepancy from ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} if it exists, with no restrictions are placed on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. In this case, if we choose W1W_{1} as independent beta priors on θa\theta_{a} and θb\theta_{b}, we can simply proceed as described in Proposition 2 above, taking a beta prior for simplicity. We will develop a reasonable ‘default’ choice for the hyper parameters by experiment in Section 5.

4.1 Dealing with Effect Sizes

In the second scenario we really want to test ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} against a restricted ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} consisting of those hypotheses that have a certain minimal effect size δ\delta. This would then be a one-sided test. For example, a researcher might know that a new treatment must cure at least a certain number of patients more compared to a control treatment to provide a clinically relevant treatment effect δ\delta. In this case, ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} could be restricted to either of the sets Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta) or Θ+​(δ)\Theta^{+}(\delta), where

Θ(δ)={θ∈[0,1]2:d(θ)=δ};Θ+(δ)={{θ∈[0,1]2:d⁡(θ)≥δ}if δ>0{θ∈[0,1]2:d⁡(θ)≤δ}if δ<0,\Theta(\delta)=\left\{\theta\in[0,1]^{2}:d(\theta)=\delta\right\}\ \ ;\ \ \Theta^{+}(\delta)=\begin{cases}\left\{\theta\in[0,1]^{2}:d(\theta)\geq\delta\right\}&\text{if $\delta>0$}\\ \left\{\theta\in[0,1]^{2}:d(\theta)\leq\delta\right\}&\text{if $\delta<0$,}\end{cases} (4.1)

where we set d⁡((θa,θb))=θb−θad((\theta_{a},\theta_{b}))=\theta_{b}-\theta_{a}. A second notion of effect size that often will be applicable in this sort of research is the log odds ratio between θb\theta_{b} and θa\theta_{a}, with restricted parameter space again given by (4.1) but dd set to

d⁡((θa,θb))=log⁡(θb1−θb⋅1−θaθa).d((\theta_{a},\theta_{b}))=\log\left(\frac{\theta_{b}}{1-\theta_{b}}\cdot\frac{1-\theta_{a}}{\theta_{a}}\right). (4.2)

These are the two effect size notions that will feature in our experiments. An illustration of both divergence measures and the resulting restricted parameter spaces is given in Figure 1.

A third popular notion of effect size, the relative risk, behaves, for small θa\theta_{a} and δ>0\delta>0, very similarly to the odds ratio, and will therefore not be separately considered in our experiments.

If we pick ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} restrict to Θ⁡(δ′)\Theta(\delta^{\prime}), then we could simply use the beta prior mentioned before with support conditioned on this set. What about the more realistic case of a ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} with δ∈Θ+​(δ′)\delta\in\Theta^{+}(\delta^{\prime})? A first, intuitive (and certainly defensible) approach would be to use a prior W1′W^{\prime}_{1} that is spread out over Θ+​(δ′)\Theta^{+}(\delta^{\prime}), e.g. (if δ′>0\delta^{\prime}>0) the beta prior as above conditioned on δ≥δ\delta\geq\delta. However, in terms of the GRO criterion, there are good reasons to still use a prior W1∗W^{*}_{1} that puts all prior mass on Θ⁡(δ′)\Theta(\delta^{\prime}), the boundary of the real parameter space Θ⁡(δ+)\Theta(\delta^{+}). Namely, for the resulting 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable process S[na,nb,W1∗](1),S[na,nb,W1∗](2),…S^{(1)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W^{*}_{1}]},S^{(2)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W^{*}_{1}]},\ldots, it holds for every mm that

for all (θa,θb) with d⁡((θa,θb))>δ′,𝐄Y(m)∼P(θa,θb)​[log⁡S[na,nb,W1∗](m)]≥minθ∈Θ⁡(δ′)⁡𝐄Y(m)∼Pθ​[log⁡S[na,nb,W1∗](m)].\text{for all $(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})$ with $d((\theta_{a},\theta_{b}))>\delta^{\prime}$},\ {\bf E}_{Y^{(m)}\sim P_{(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})}}[\log S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W^{*}_{1}]}]\geq\\ \min_{\theta\in\Theta(\delta^{\prime})}{\bf E}_{Y^{(m)}\sim P_{\theta}}[\log S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W^{*}_{1}]}]. (4.3)

Thus, we might want to use the prior W1∗W^{*}_{1} also if δ\delta can be more extreme than δ′\delta^{\prime}, since if δ\delta is actually more extreme, the expected (log-) evidence against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} using W1∗W_{1}^{*} (even though designed for δ′\delta^{\prime}) will actually get larger anyway.

The advantage of the first approach is that it will lead to much higher GROwth (𝐄P(θa,θb)​[log⁡S[na,nb,W1′](m)]{\bf E}_{P_{(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})}}[\log S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W^{\prime}_{1}]}] much larger than 𝐄P(θa,θb)​[log⁡S[na,nb,W1∗](m)]{\bf E}_{P_{(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})}}[\log S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W^{*}_{1}]}]) if we are ‘lucky’ and |d⁡(θa,θb)|≫|δ′||d(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})|\gg|\delta^{\prime}|. The price to pay is that it will lead to somewhat smaller growth if d⁡((θa,θb))d((\theta_{a},\theta_{b})) is (still arger than but) close to δ′\delta^{\prime} (experiments omitted). It is easy to see why: the prior W1′W^{\prime}_{1} must spread out its mass over a much larger subset of [0,1]2[0,1]^{2} than W1∗W^{*}_{1}. Therefore, the E-variables based on W1′W^{\prime}_{1} will perform somewhat worse than those based on W1∗W^{*}_{1} if the data are sampled from a point (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta_{b}^{*}) in the support of W1∗W^{*}_{1}, simply because W1∗W^{*}_{1} gives much larger prior support in a neighborhood of (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta_{b}^{*}). For this reason, and also because it is computationally a lot simpler, we decided to focus our experiments on the second approach rather than the first.

Calculating the prior and posterior for restricted ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}

For both notions of effect size, θa\theta_{a} and θb\theta_{b} can no longer be independent for any prior on Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta). Hence, the prior and posterior do not longer admit the composition in terms of beta densities as in Proposition 2. For example, when putting a prior on Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta) with the additive effect size notion, we know the new domain of θa\theta_{a} would be [0,1−δ][0,1-\delta]. θb\theta_{b} is completely determined by θa\theta_{a} and δ\delta in this case. We will still use a beta prior on Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta) and calculate posteriors by a numerical approach, explained in Appendix S1 of the Supplementary Material.

4.2 Working with Restrictions on event rate

In practice, researchers often already have estimates of the occurrence rate of events in the control group in their experiments; for example, estimates of the proportion of patients that recover from a disease under standard care are known, and researchers investigate whether the proportion of recovered patients is higher in a group receiving an experimental treatment. This restriction on θa\theta_{a} can be incorporated in the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable. This incorporation becomes especially easy if ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is already restricted to a set Θ+​(δ′)\Theta^{+}(\delta^{\prime}) with minimal relevant effect size δ′\delta^{\prime}. For then Θ⁡(δ′)\Theta(\delta^{\prime}) contains just one point (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta_{a}^{*},\theta_{b}^{*}) (in the case of the linear effect size, this is (θa,θa+δ)(\theta_{a},\theta_{a}+\delta)), and the 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable constructed according to the guidelines of the previous subsection, which puts all its mass on δ′\delta^{\prime} even though we allow δ≥δ′\delta\geq\delta^{\prime}, would be the generic 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable corresponding to putting prior mass 1 on (θa∗,θb∗)(\theta_{a}^{*},\theta_{b}^{*}).

5 Illustration via Simulated Data

In this section, we illustrate properties of our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables for 2×22\times 2 application through simulated data, generated with our software package publicly available through Github (Ly et al.,, 2020). First, we determine a reasonable choice of beta prior hyper-parameter to use in (3.4) in terms of the GRO-criterion. Thereafter, we show by more simulations that our proposal for the beta prior hyper-parameter based on GRO also performs well in terms of power (recall from Section 1.1 that while we cannot optimize for power directly, we do want procedures with reasonable power). Finally, we compare the power of our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable with this default prior choice and different restrictions on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} to Fisher’s exact test.

REGROW

For simplicity, in all our experiments we will invariably set the beta prior hyper-parameters to αa=αb=βa=βb=γ\alpha_{a}=\alpha_{b}=\beta_{a}=\beta_{b}=\gamma for some γ>0\gamma>0 (recall that any such choice leads to a valid 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable). We will aim for the γ\gamma that minimizes (1.8) in the worst-case over all θ1∗∈[0,1]2\theta^{*}_{1}\in[0,1]^{2}, thereby following the REGROW (relative growth-rate optimality in worst-case) criterion of Grünwald et al., (2022), who give a minimax regret motivation for this choice. In essence, the prior minimizing, among all distributions over [0,1]2[0,1]^{2}, the maximum of (1.8) over all θ1∗\theta^{*}_{1} can be viewed as the prior that allows us to learn θ1∗\theta^{*}_{1} as fast as possible (based on a minimal sample) in the worst-case. Here we are contented to adopt a sub-optimal but computationally convenient prior by restricting the minimum to be over a 1-dimensional family of beta priors with hyper parameter γ\gamma. We find the minimizing γ\gamma by experiment: results are depicted in Figure 2. It depends on mm, which is unknown in advance, but for large mm, in the setting with na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1, it converges to γ≈0.18\gamma\approx 0.18, and this is the value we will take as our default choice — our experiments below indicate that it remains a good choice, also when our main concern is power, and also under restrictions on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}.

Power

Whereas GROwth is the natural performance measure in experiments that may always be continued at some point in the future, traditionally oriented researchers may be more interested in power. The question is then whether the optimal asymptotic choice γ≈0.18\gamma\approx 0.18 in terms of the relative GRO property for unrestricted ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is also the optimal choice in terms of power (which is usually considered in combination with some minimal effect size, i.e. a restricted ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}). The following experiment shows that by and large it is. For simplicity we only illustrate the case na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1 and a desired power of 0.80.8. For various effect sizes δ\delta, and various values of γ\gamma, we first determined the smallest sample size (number of blocks) mm such that, under optional stopping up until and including mm, the power is ≥0.8\geq 0.8 in the worst case over all (θa,θb)(\theta_{a},\theta_{b}) with δ=θb−θa\delta=\theta_{b}-\theta_{a}. Here by ‘optional stopping up until and including mm’, we mean ‘we stop and reject the null iff S(m′)[na,nb,W[γ]>α−1S^{(m^{\prime})}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W_{[\gamma]}}>\alpha^{-1} for some m′∈{1,2,…,mm^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\ldots,m}, and we stop and accept the null if this is not the case (so mm is the maximal sample size we consider)’. We call this mm the worst-case sample size needed for 80%80\% power at effect size δ\delta with prior parameter γ\gamma. The reason for calling it worst-case is that in practice, by engaging in optional stopping with a fixed maximal sample size, the expected sample size of this procedure is smaller: if, for m′<mm^{\prime}<m, we already have S(m′)[na,nb,W[γ]>α−1S^{(m^{\prime})}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W_{[\gamma]}}>\alpha^{-1} then we stop and reject early; if not, we go on until we have seen mm blocks and then stop (and reject iff S(m)[na,nb,W[γ]>α−1S^{(m)}_{[n_{a},n_{b},W_{[\gamma]}}>\alpha^{-1}). We thus performed two simulation experiments: first, to estimate the worst-case sample size (at α=0.05\alpha=0.05), and second, to estimate the expected sample size. Again, the estimates were obtained by re-simulating a sequence of data blocks KK times for a large number of KK, making sure the bias and variance of the estimates were sufficiently small.

In Figure 3 results of these experiments are depicted. We make two observations: first, almost no difference in sample sizes to plan for between γ=0.18\gamma=0.18 and γ=0.05\gamma=0.05 was observed for distributions with small expected sample sizes (represented by the triangles and the dots, which overlap for most data points), and other values of γ\gamma obtained smaller power, indicating that the relative growth-optimal γ=0.18\gamma=0.18 could in practice be used as a default setting for our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable — and as a consequence, we recommend it as such. Second, in the rightmost panel we see that for distributions with very small relative differences between θa\theta_{a} and θb\theta_{b}, e.g. P0.5,0.58P_{0.5,0.58}, values of γ\gamma higher than 0.180.18 yielded a higher power, whereas for such δ\delta, the relative GROW criterion was optimized for γ=0.18\gamma=0.18 for the corresponding (very large) stopping times in our simulation experiments. This is not surprising given what is known for simple ℋ0={Pθ0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\theta_{0}}\}: when testing a point null θ0\theta_{0} with a 1-dimensional exponential family alternative, safe tests based on Bayes factors with standard Bayesian (e.g. Gaussian or conjugate) priors do not obtain optimal power in an asymptotic sense: they reject if |θ^−θ0|2≳(log⁡n)/n|\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0}|^{2}\gtrsim(\log n)/n (with θ^\hat{\theta} denoting the MLE; see the example on ZZ-tests by Grünwald et al., (2022)) whereas based on nonstandard ‘switching’ (van der Pas and Grünwald,, 2018) or ‘stitching’ methods (Howard et al.,, 2021), corresponding to special priors with densities going to infinity as effect size goes to 00, one can get rejection if |θ^−θ0|2≳(log⁡log⁡n)/n|\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0}|^{2}\gtrsim(\log\log n)/n. However, there is a significant price to pay in terms of the constants hidden in the asymptotics, and in practice, ‘standard’ priors may very well perform better at all but very large sample sizes (Maillard,, 2019). Given that the higher γ\gamma, the more the beta prior behaves like a switch prior, we conjecture that what we see in Figure 3(b) at very small δ\delta is a version of the switching/stitching phenomenon with a composite null; since it only kicks in at very large sample sizes, we prefer γ=0.18\gamma=0.18 as the default choice after all.

Finally, we compared the performance of our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables with the “default” beta priors with γ=0.18\gamma=0.18 with their classical counterpart, Fisher’s exact test. We show that with Fisher’s exact test, type-I error probability guarantee is lost, whereas with the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables it remains bounded — since these results are exactly as would be expected from the theory they have been placed in the supplementary material (Figure S3.1 in Appendix S3 in the Supporting Material). In the main text below, we compare worst-case and expected stopping times of the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables with- and without restrictions on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} for sample sizes one would need to plan for when analyzing experiment results with Fisher’s exact test; see Figure 4. We noticed that the expected sample sizes achieved under optional stopping with the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable with unrestricted ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} were very similar to the sample sizes needed to plan for with Fisher’s exact test. When using a correctly specified restriction on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} (the leftmost data points in the second and third subfigures), this expected number of samples is even considerably lower than the sample size to plan for with Fisher’s exact test. However, under misspecification, when the difference or log odds ratio used in the design of the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable turns out to be a lot smaller than the real difference present in the data generating machinery, one should expect to collect more samples (the data points towards the right in the second subfigure). This effect would disappear if we were to put a prior on the full Θ+​(δ)\Theta^{+}(\delta) rather than the boundary Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta), at the price of slightly worse behaviour in the well-specified case when data is sampled from Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta).

Note that in Figure 4 we used the default beta prior parameters γ=0.18\gamma=0.18 found optimal for the unrestricted case for the restricted cases as well; some first experiments revealed that changing the prior parameter values did not lead to significant changes in power for the restricted 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables (results not shown). We do however offer the possibility in our software package (Ly et al.,, 2020) to run similar experiments for users to determine the optimal prior parameter γ\gamma for a given expected sample size and Θ(+)​(δ′)\Theta^{(+)}(\delta^{\prime}).

Beyond Two-Stream Data: Safe Tests for KK Proportions

We also compared the performance of the extended version of our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for kk Bernoulli data streams to the corresponding classical, nonsequential counterpart, the chi-square test (McHugh,, 2013). In this setting, we have a k×2k\times 2 contingency table test, where we test whether kk Bernoulli data streams come from the same source. The extension of (3.4) to kk data streams analogously to (2.4) is straightforward. Our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable with uniform priors significantly outperforms the chi-square test for small sample sizes and large effect sizes (see Figure 5), probably explained by the fact that the chi-square test is not exact, but the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable is. For expected cell counts smaller than 55 the chi-square test should not be used, reflected in an increased number of samples needed for similar power (McHugh,, 2013).

6 Illustration via Real World Data

We will now demonstrate the approach through a real-world example: the SWEPIS study on labor induction (Wennerholm et al.,, 2019). Wagenmakers and Ly, (2020) have used this example before to illustrate how using single p-values to make decisions can hide valuable information in research data.

In the SWEPIS study, two groups of pregnant women were followed. In the first group labor was induced at 41 weeks, and in the second labor was induced after 42 weeks. The study was stopped early, as 6 cases of stillbirth were observed in the 42-weeks group (at nb=1379n_{b}=1379), as compared to 0 in the 41-weeks group (at na=1381n_{a}=1381). These data yield a significant Fisher’s exact test, P≈0.015P\approx 0.015, for testing that the number of stillbirths in the 42-weeks group is higher, when (wrongly) assuming that nan_{a} and nbn_{b} were fixed in advance to the above values.

If we had used 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables for continuously analyzing this data, would we then have found evidence for superiority of the 41 weeks approach, and would we have stopped the study earlier? As the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables we propose are not exchangeable, i.e. their values change under permutations of the data sequences, a direct comparison to the results of the SWEPIS study is not possible as the exact data stream is not available. To simulate a “real-time” scenario equivalent to the SWEPIS study, we assume we collect a total of 13801380 data blocks, with na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1, with a total of 27602760 observations. We already know that in group a, 00 events are observed. In group b, 66 events are observed, of which we know that the last event was observed in data block 13801380, directly before the study was stopped. Hence, we can simulate the “real-time” data by permuting the indices of the observations in group b in the 13791379 first data blocks.

Four different approaches for analyzing the data with 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables were explored: without any restriction on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, with a restriction based on the additive divergence measure (the minimal difference between the groups), with a restriction based on the log odds ratio, and with a restriction on the event rate in the control group and on the minimal difference. The minimal difference, log odds ratio and event rate used were chosen based on a large recent meta-analysis on stillbirths (Muglu et al.,, 2019); we used δ=0.00318\delta=0.00318 as a restriction on the difference between the groups, log⁡(2)\log(2) for the log odds ratio and 0.00010.0001 as the event rate. For all 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables, the default beta prior hyperparameters with γ=0.18\gamma=0.18 as earlier were used.

In Figure 6 the spread of the evidence collected with the four types of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables in 10001000 simulations analogous to the SWEPIS setting is depicted. Because the observed effect size was higher than expected, 𝙴\mathtt{E}-values obtained with the (too low) restriction on the effect size were lower than the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-values obtained with the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable without restrictions. Adding the restriction on the event rate increased the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-values, and in all 1000 simulations, the SWEPIS study would have been stopped before the occurrence of the sixth stillbirth. Figure 6 also depicts results of a second simulation experiment, where we sampled 10001000 data streams from P0,6/1380P_{0,6/1380} and recorded the stopping times while analyzing the streams with the four 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables with different restrictions on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. With the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables without restriction, or with a restriction on the event rate and difference between the groups, we would have often stopped data collection earlier than in the SWEPIS setting.

We can thus conclude that, would the monitoring of the study have been performed with 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables instead of p-values, first of all we would have collected correct evidence for a higher proportion of stillbirths in the 42-weeks group, and second, the degree of evidence is quite similar to that collected with the (incorrectly determined) p-value: both are significant at the 0.050.05 level. Wagemakers and Ly with their method also found evidence for the existence of a difference between the two groups, but not nearly of the same degree: they reported Bayes factors that varied, depending on the choice of the prior, between 11 and 5.45.4 (note that whenever we reject, our product of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-values, which like a Bayes factor can be thought of as a prequential likelihood ratio, must be ≥20\geq 20). A possible explanation for this difference could be that the Bayes factors used for collecting evidence in their study are not designed for analyzing stream data. As we also saw in our experiments, choosing the wrong prior or restriction on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} can make a large difference for the evidence collected. These results show that when planning a prospective study, using 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables for analysis could, through their flexibility, contribute to earlier evidence collection compared to existing methods.

7 Other 𝙴\mathtt{E}-Variables for Two Data Streams

7.1 The GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for some Exponential and Location Families

The simplification (3.2) shows that in the Bernoulli case with simple Θ1={(θa∗,θb∗)}\Theta_{1}=\{(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b})\}, we can take in our denominator pθ0p_{\theta_{0}} with θ0=nan​θa∗+nbn​θb∗\theta_{0}=\frac{n_{a}}{n}\theta^{*}_{a}+\frac{n_{b}}{n}\theta^{*}_{b} — which can also be interpreted as the distribution in the null corresponding to a mixture of the means, rather than the mixture of two distributions in the null. The Bernoulli model is a special case of 1-parameter exponential families which can all be parameterized in terms of their means so that Θ⊂𝐑\Theta\subset\mathbf{R} and 𝐄Pθ​[Y]=θ{\bf E}_{P_{\theta}}[Y]=\theta; this is also possible for some location families that are not of exponential form. This suggests that, for all such models, instead of (2.2) we might also consider the likelihood ratio (3.2). For the Bernoulli model, both definitions will coincide, but for general 1-parameter exponential families they do not since their corresponding set of densities is not convex. The question is now whether (3.2) defines an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for general exponential families. It turns out that the answer is no in general, but yes in some special cases. For a negative example, consider the case with Θ=𝐑+\Theta=\mathbf{R}^{+} representing the family of exponential distributions in their mean-value parameterization, i.e. pθ​(y)=λ​exp⁡(−λ​y)p_{\theta}(y)=\lambda\exp(-\lambda y) with λ=1/θ\lambda=1/\theta and take na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1. A simple calculation shows that for any θa∗≠θb∗∈Θ\theta^{*}_{a}\neq\theta^{*}_{b}\in\Theta, we have limθ→∞𝐄Ya,Yb​ i.i.d.∼Pθ​[pθa∗​(Ya)​pθb∗​(Yb)/p(θa∗+θb∗)/2​(Ya,Yb)]=∞\lim_{\theta\rightarrow\infty}{\bf E}_{Y_{a},Y_{b}\text{\ i.i.d.}\sim P_{\theta}}[p_{\theta^{*}_{a}}(Y_{a})p_{\theta^{*}_{b}}(Y_{b})/p_{(\theta^{*}_{a}+\theta^{*}_{b})/2}(Y_{a},Y_{b})]=\infty. The negative binomial families provide, by a similar calculation, another negative example. For a positive example, consider the case with Θ=𝐑\Theta=\mathbf{R} representing the Gaussian location family with fixed variance 11 and again take na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1. A simple calculation shows that (3.2) is equal to the likelihood ratio for testing whether the difference Z=Ya−YbZ=Y_{a}-Y_{b} is a Gaussian with variance 2\sqrt{2} with either mean 00 or mean θb−θa\theta_{b}-\theta_{a}. This is in fact the standard paired-sample ZZ-test that would normally be advised in this situation. In fact it is the GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for this situation:

Proposition 3.

Let {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} represent a family of probability distributions with densities pθp_{\theta}, with Θ\Theta a convex set in 𝐑k\mathbf{R}^{k} for some k≥1k\geq 1. For any θa∗,θb∗∈Θ\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b}\in\Theta we have: if (3.2) is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Θ1={(θa∗,θb∗)}\Theta_{1}=\{(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b})\} then it is the GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Θ1={(θa∗,θb∗)}\Theta_{1}=\{(\theta^{*}_{a},\theta^{*}_{b})\}.

The proof is immediate from Proposition 1. The proposition implies that in the special cases in which (3.2) does provide an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable, it is to be preferred (achieves better growth) above our original construction (2.2). (2.2) has the advantage that it provides an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable relative to arbitrary models. We plan to study the cases in which (3.2) can be used instead in future work.

7.2 The Conditional 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Tests of Two Proportions

Wald, (1947) proposed a 2-sample sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) for the 2×22\times 2 setting. Since SPRTs can be written in terms of products of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables (although products of 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables often do not give SPRTs; see the discussion by Grünwald et al., (2022)), let us see what 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables Wald’s test corresponds to. The setting is restricted to size-2 blocks with na=nb=1n_{a}=n_{b}=1. We measure effect size with dd the log-odds ratio (4.2) and consider an alternative with a d⁡(θa,θb)d(\theta_{a},\theta_{b}) that is at least some given δ\delta. Using that, for all (θa,θb)∈(0,1)2(\theta_{a},\theta_{b})\in(0,1)^{2}, z∈{0,1,2}z\in\{0,1,2\}, the conditional probability mass function pθa,θb​(Ya,Yb∣∑Ya+Yb=z)p_{\theta_{a},\theta_{b}}(Y_{a},Y_{b}\mid\sum Y_{a}+Y_{b}=z) only depends on the log-odds ratio, we can write it, as qδ​(ya,yb|z)q_{\delta}(y_{a},y_{b}|z) where qδq_{\delta} is a probability mass function whose definition depends on (θa,θb)(\theta_{a},\theta_{b}) only via δ=d⁡((θa,θb))\delta=d((\theta_{a},\theta_{b})). We then take as our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable Scond,δ:=qδ​(Ya,Yb∣Ya+Yb)/q0​(Ya,Yb∣Ya+Yb)S_{\textsc{cond},\delta}:=q_{\delta}(Y_{a},Y_{b}\mid Y_{a}+Y_{b})/q_{0}(Y_{a},Y_{b}\mid Y_{a}+Y_{b}). Since the conditional distribution q0​(Ya,Yb∣Z)q_{0}(Y_{a},Y_{b}\mid Z) is the same for all distributions in the null, this conditional likelihood gives an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable and can be used instead of our generic 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable. Since for this Bernoulli case, our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable is in fact GRO, we would expect this new conditional 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable to perform worse in terms of GRO (and for the reasons given in Section 1.1 also in terms of the amount of data needed before one can reject at a desired power), and experiments (not reported here) confirm that it indeed performs slightly worse for δ\delta close to 00, and substantially worse for larger δ\delta. This is already suggested by the fact that, unlike the GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable, Scond,δS_{\textsc{cond},\delta} takes on value 11 whenever ya=yby_{a}=y_{b}, effectively ignoring data blocks in which both outcomes are the same. Another disadvantage is that it can only be used in combination with effect size given by the odds ratio or any monotonic transformation thereof; whereas the GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable can also be combined with the difference θb−θa\theta_{b}-\theta_{a} or any other desirable notion of effect size.

8 Conclusion

We have established 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables and test martingales for the general two-i.i.d.-data streams problem. We have demonstrated, using theory, simulations and a real-world example that, for tests of two proportions, by choosing an appropriate prior on Θ1\Theta_{1}, the method can be made competitive with classical methods that do not allow for optional stopping. Whereas in this paper, we have focused on testing, our 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables can also be extended to get anytime-valid confidence sequences (Howard et al.,, 2021; Lai,, 1976), i.e. confidence sequences for effect sizes that are valid even under optional stopping. This requires us to first extend the testing to scenarios with δ≥δ1\delta\geq\delta_{1} vs. δ≤δ0\delta\leq\delta_{0} for δ0≠0\delta_{0}\neq 0, that is, null hypotheses with θa≠θb\theta_{a}\neq\theta_{b}. We will report on this extension elsewhere. Our work also suggests a question for future work that is practically relevant, easy to state but hard to answer: to what extent do our findings generalize to logistic regression?

Appendix: Proofs

The proofs below repeatedly use Theorem 1 of Grünwald et al., (2022) and a direct corollary (called Corollary 2 by Grünwald et al., (2022)), which we re-state here, for convenience, combined as a single statement. We use the notation adopted later in the paper: for ℋ0={Pθ:θ∈Θ0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{0}\} and, for WW a distribution on Θ0\Theta_{0}, we write PW=∫Pθ​𝑑W​(θ)P_{W}=\int P_{\theta}dW(\theta).

Theorem (Theorem 1 of Grünwald et al., (2022))

Let YY be a random variable taking values in a set 𝒴{\cal Y}. Suppose QQ is a probability distribution for YY with density qq that is strictly positive on all of 𝒴{\cal Y} and let ℋ0={Pθ:θ∈Θ0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{0}\} be a set of distributions for YY where each PθP_{\theta} has density pθp_{\theta}. Let 𝒲0{\cal W}_{0} be the set all distributions on Θ0\Theta_{0}. Assume infW0∈𝒲0​(Θ0)D(Q∥PW0)<∞\inf_{W_{0}\in{\cal W}_{0}(\Theta_{0})}D(Q\|P_{W_{0}})<\infty. Then (a) there exists a (potentially sub-) distribution P0∗P^{*}_{0} with density p0∗p^{*}_{0} such that

S∗:=q⁡(Y)p0∗​(Y)S^{*}:=\frac{q(Y)}{p^{*}_{0}(Y)}

is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable (p0∗p^{*}_{0} is called the Reverse Information Projection (RIPr) of qq onto {pW:W∈𝒲0}\{p_{W}:W\in{\cal W}_{0}\} (Li,, 1999; Li and Barron,, 2000; Grünwald et al.,, 2019)). Moreover, (b), S∗S^{*} satisfies

supS∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)𝐄Y∼Q[logS]=𝐄Y∼Q[logS∗]=infW0∈𝒲0​(Θ0)D(Q∥PW0)=D(Q∥P0∗).\displaystyle\sup_{S\in{\cal E}(\Theta_{0})}{\bf E}_{Y\sim Q}[\log S]={\bf E}_{Y\sim Q}[\log S^{*}]=\inf_{W_{0}\in{\cal W}_{0}(\Theta_{0})}D(Q\|P_{W_{0}})=D(Q\|P^{*}_{0}). (8.1)

and is thus the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for YY. If the minimum is achieved by some W0∗{W}^{*}_{0}, i.e. D(Q∥P0∗)=D(Q∥PW0∗)D(Q\|P^{*}_{0})=D(Q\|P_{W^{*}_{0}}), then P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W^{*}_{0}}. Moreover, (c), if there exists an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable SS of the form q​(Y)/pW0​(Y)q(Y)/p_{W_{0}}(Y) for some W0∈𝒲0W_{0}\in{\cal W}_{0} then W0W_{0} must achieve the infimum in (8.1) and SS must be essentially equal to S∗S^{*} in the sense that for all P∈ℋ0∪{Q}P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}\cup\{Q\}, P⁡(S∗=q⁡(Y)/pW0​(Y))=1P(S^{*}=q(Y)/p_{W_{0}}(Y))=1. Similarly (d), if there exists a W0∗∈𝒲0W^{*}_{0}\in{\cal W}_{0} that achieves the infimum in (8.1) then S=q⁡(Y)/pW0∗​(Y)S=q(Y)/p_{W^{*}_{0}}(Y) is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable and SS is again essentially equal to S∗S^{*}.

8.1 Proof of Propositions

Proof of Proposition 1

Below we state and prove a slight generalization of Proposition 1.

Proposition 4.

Let ℋ1={Q}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{Q\} be a singleton and let ℋ0={Pθ:θ∈Θ0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{0}\} be such that for some distribution WW on Θ0\Theta_{0}, D(Q∥PW)<∞D(Q\|P_{W})<\infty. For general θ∈Θ0\theta\in\Theta_{0} and distributions WW on Θ0\Theta_{0}, define Sθ,(j):=q⁡(Y(j))/pθ​(Y(j))S_{\theta,(j)}:=q(Y_{(j)})/p_{\theta}(Y_{(j)}) and SW,(j)=q⁡(Y(j))/pW​(Y(j)).S_{W,(j)}=q(Y_{(j)})/p_{W}(Y_{(j)}). We have:

  1. 1.

    Suppose there exists a distribution WW on Θ0\Theta_{0} such that SW,(1)S_{W,(1)} is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable. Then SW,(1)S_{W,(1)} is the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Y(1)Y_{(1)}. In particular, if WW puts mass 11 on a particular θ∘∈Θ0\theta^{\circ}\in\Theta_{0}, then SW,(1)=Sθ∘,(1)S_{W,(1)}=S_{\theta^{\circ},(1)} is the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable.

  2. 2.

    If Θ0={θ0}\Theta_{0}=\{\theta_{0}\} is simple then, with the prior W0W_{0} putting mass 1 on θ0\theta_{0}, SW0,(1)=Sθ0,(1)S_{W_{0},(1)}=S_{\theta_{0},(1)} is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable and hence, by the above, also the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable.

  3. 3.

    If, for some θ∘∈Θ0\theta^{\circ}\in\Theta_{0}, Sθ∘,(1)S_{\theta^{\circ},(1)} is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable and we further assume that Y(1),Y(2),…Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)},\ldots are i.i.d. according to all distributions in ℋ0∪ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{0}\cup\mathcal{H}_{1}, then Sgro​(Q)(m)=∏j=1mSθ∘,(j)S^{(m)}_{\text{\sc gro}(Q)}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{\theta^{\circ},(j)}; that is, the QQ-GRO optimal (unconditional) 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Y(m)Y^{(m)} is the product of the individual QQ-GRO optimal 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables.

Proof.

Part 1 The theorem above, part (b), implies, with Y=Y(1)Y=Y_{(1)}, that some QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable S∗S^{*} for Y(1)Y_{(1)} exists. Part (c) then implies that we can take S∗S^{*} to be equal to SW,(1)S_{W,(1)}. This implies the statement.

Part 2 is immediate. Part 3 We assume that Sθ∘,(1)S_{\theta^{\circ},(1)} is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}–variable. Then the i.i.d. assumption implies that Sθ∘(m):=∏j=1mSθ∘,(j)=∏q⁡(Y(j))/pθ∘​(Y(j))S_{\theta^{\circ}}^{(m)}:=\prod_{j=1}^{m}S_{\theta^{\circ},(j)}=\prod q(Y_{(j)})/p_{\theta^{\circ}}(Y_{(j)}) is also an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable. But (Grünwald et al.,, 2019, Theorem 1), part (c) as stated above implies (by taking a distribution WW putting mass 11 on θ\theta) that for ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} for which data are i.i.d., for each m≥1m\geq 1, that if a θ∈Θ0\theta\in\Theta_{0} exists such that Sθ(m)S_{\theta}^{(m)} is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable, then Sθ(m)S_{\theta}^{(m)} must be the QQ-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable for Y(m)Y^{(m)}. This proves the statement. ∎

=11+κ​Ua+Ub+(1+κ)​αana​(j−1)+αa+βa=U+(1+κ)​αan⁡(j−1)+(1+κ)​αa+(1+κ)​βa,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1+\kappa}\frac{U_{a}+U_{b}+(1+\kappa)\alpha_{a}}{n_{a}(j-1)+\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a}}=\frac{U+(1+\kappa)\alpha_{a}}{n(j-1)+(1+\kappa)\alpha_{a}+(1+\kappa)\beta_{a}},

8.2 Proof of Theorem 1

We first restate Theorem 1 in its extended version that holds for k≥2k\geq 2 data streams. Let n→=(n1,…,nk),n=∑g=1kng,θ→=(θa,…,θk)∈Θk\vec{n}=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}),n=\sum_{g=1}^{k}n_{g},\vec{\theta}=(\theta_{a},\ldots,\theta_{k})\in\Theta^{k} and y→n\vec{y}^{n} be as above (2.4). We use ‘Y→n∼Pθ∗\vec{Y}^{n}\sim P_{\theta^{*}}’ as an abbreviation for ‘ Y1n1∼Pθ1∗;…;Yknk∼Pθk∗Y_{1}^{n_{1}}\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{1}};\ldots;Y_{k}^{n_{k}}\sim P_{\theta^{*}_{k}}’.

Theorem 1.

Let

s⁡(y→n,n→,θ→∗)≔∏g=1kpθg∗​(ygng)∏i=1ng(∑g′=1kng′n​pθg′∗​(yi,g)).s(\vec{y}^{n};\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*})\coloneqq\prod_{g=1}^{k}\frac{p_{\theta_{g}^{*}}(y^{n_{g}}_{g})}{\prod_{i=1}^{n_{g}}\left(\sum_{g^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{n_{g^{\prime}}}{n}p_{\theta^{*}_{g^{\prime}}}(y_{i,g})\right)}.

The random variable S[n→,θ→∗]:=s⁡(Y→n,n→,θ→∗)S_{[\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*}]}:=s(\vec{Y}^{n};\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*}) is an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable, i.e. we have:

supθ∈Θ𝐄Vn∼Pθ​[s⁡(Vn,n→,θ→∗)]≤1.\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}{\bf E}_{V^{n}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[s(V^{n};\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*})\right]\leq 1.

Moreover, if {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} is a convex set of distributions, then S[n→,θ→∗]S_{[\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*}]} is the (θ→∗)(\vec{\theta}^{*})-GRO 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variable: for any non-negative function s′s^{\prime} on 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}^{n} satisfying supθ∈Θ𝐄Vn∼Pθ​[s′​(Vn)]≤1\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}{\bf E}_{V^{n}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[s^{\prime}(V^{n})\right]\leq 1, we have:

𝐄Y→n∼Pθ∗​[log⁡s⁡(Y→n,n→,θ→∗)]≥𝐄Y→n∼Pθ∗​[log⁡s′​(Y→n)].{\bf E}_{\vec{Y}^{n}\sim P_{\theta^{*}}}[\log s(\vec{Y}^{n};\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*})]\geq{\bf E}_{\vec{Y}^{n}\sim P_{\theta^{*}}}[\log s^{\prime}(\vec{Y}^{n})].

Proof of Theorem 1

The following fact plays a central role in the proof:

Fact

For g∈(1,…,k)g\in(1,...,k), let ng∈𝐍,n:=∑g=1kngn_{g}\in\mathbf{N},n:=\sum_{g=1}^{k}n_{g} and let ug∈𝐑+u_{g}\in\mathbf{R}^{+}. Suppose that ∑g=1kng​ug≤n\sum_{g=1}^{k}n_{g}u_{g}\leq n. Then ∏g=1kugng≤1\prod_{g=1}^{k}u_{g}^{n_{g}}\leq 1.

This result follows from the following standard generalization of Young’s inequality to kk numbers: for any kk numbers u1,…,uk∈𝐑0+u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}\in\mathbf{R}^{+}_{0} and any kk nonnegative numbers p1,…,pkp_{1},\ldots,p_{k} with ∑g=1kpg=1\sum_{g=1}^{k}p_{g}=1, we have ∏g=1kugpg≤∑g=1kpg​ug\prod_{g=1}^{k}u_{g}^{p_{g}}\leq\sum_{g=1}^{k}p_{g}u_{g}. Applying this with pg=ng/np_{g}=n_{g}/n to ugu_{g} and ngn_{g} as above, we get ∏g=1kugng/n≤∑g=1k(ng​ug)/n≤1\prod_{g=1}^{k}u_{g}^{n_{g}/n}\leq\sum_{g=1}^{k}(n_{g}u_{g})/n\leq 1, and the result follows by exponentiating to the power nn.
Part 1 For y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, set set p∘​(y):=∑g=1k(ng/n)​pθg∗​(y)p^{\circ}(y):=\sum_{g=1}^{k}(n_{g}/n)p_{\theta^{*}_{g}}(y) and p∘​(ym)=∏i=1mp∘​(yi)p^{\circ}(y^{m})=\prod_{i=1}^{m}p^{\circ}(y_{i}). For all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta we have:

𝐄Vn∼Pθ​[s⁡(Vn,n→,θ→∗)]=∏g=1k𝐄Ygng∼Pθ​[pθg∗​(Ygng)p∘​(Ygng)]=∏g=1k(𝐄Y∼Pθ​[pθg∗​(Y)p∘​(Y)])ng.\displaystyle{\bf E}_{V^{n}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[s(V^{n};\vec{n},\vec{\theta}^{*})\right]=\prod_{g=1}^{k}{\bf E}_{Y_{g}^{n_{g}}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[\frac{p_{\theta_{g}^{*}}(Y^{n_{g}}_{g})}{p^{\circ}(Y^{n_{g}}_{g})}\right]=\prod_{g=1}^{k}\left({\bf E}_{Y\sim P_{\theta}}\left[\frac{p_{\theta_{g}^{*}}(Y)}{p^{\circ}(Y)}\right]\right)^{n_{g}}. (8.3)

We also have

∑g=1kngn​𝐄Y∼Pθ​[pθg∗​(Y)p∘​(Y)]=𝐄Y∼Pθ​[∑g=1kngn⋅pθg∗​(Y)∑g′=1kng′n​pθg′∗​(Y)]=1.\displaystyle\sum_{g=1}^{k}\frac{n_{g}}{n}{\bf E}_{Y\sim P_{\theta}}\left[\frac{p_{\theta_{g}^{*}}(Y)}{p^{\circ}(Y)}\right]={\bf E}_{Y\sim P_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{g=1}^{k}\frac{n_{g}}{n}\cdot\frac{p_{\theta_{g}^{*}}(Y)}{\sum_{g^{\prime}=1}^{k}\frac{n_{g^{\prime}}}{n}p_{\theta^{*}_{g^{\prime}}}(Y)}\right]=1. (8.4)

Part 2 By convexity of {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}, there exists θ∘∈Θ\theta^{\circ}\in\Theta such that pθ∘=∑g=1k(ng/n)​pθg∗p_{\theta^{\circ}}=\sum_{g=1}^{k}(n_{g}/n)p_{\theta^{*}_{g}} and then the numerator in (2.2) can we rewritten as pθ∘​(y→)p_{\theta^{\circ}}(\vec{y}). The GRO-property is now an immediate consequence of Proposition 4, Part 1.

Appendix S1 Numerical approach to calculating 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables for restricted ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}

In this subsection we describe how we propose to approximate the beta prior and posterior on the restricted ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} with parameter space Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta), as defined in (4.1). Note that we limit ourselves to δ>0\delta>0 in this detailed description; for δ<0\delta<0 one can apply an entirely equivalent approach, with an extra term in the reparameterization. We define

ζ={δ​ if ​d​((θa,θb))=θb−θa,0​ if ​d​((θa,θb))=log-odds-ratio​(θa,θb),\zeta=\begin{cases}\delta\text{ if }d((\theta_{a},\theta_{b}))=\theta_{b}-\theta_{a},\\ 0\text{ if }d((\theta_{a},\theta_{b}))=\text{log-odds-ratio}(\theta_{a},\theta_{b}),\\ \end{cases}

such that we have θa∈(0,1−ζ)\theta_{a}\in(0,1-\zeta) and in both cases, θb\theta_{b} is completely determined by θa\theta_{a}: θb=d−1​(δ,θa)\theta_{b}=d^{-1}(\delta;\theta_{a}). Hence, our density estimation problem now becomes one-dimensional, which enables us to put a discretized prior on the restricted parameter space.

First, we discretize the parameter space Θa\Theta_{a} to a grid (a vector) with precision K,K∈(0,1−ζ)K,K\in(0,1-\zeta) and 1/K∈ℕ+1/K\in\mathbb{N}^{+}: 𝜽¯𝒂=(K,2​K,3​K,…,1−ζ)\bm{\bar{\theta}_{a}}=\left(K,2K,3K,\ldots,1-\zeta\right). Then, we reparameterize θa=(1−ζ)​ρ\theta_{a}=(1-\zeta)\rho, with ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). Then, we have 𝝆¯=(K/(1−ζ),2​K/(1−ζ),…,1).\bm{\bar{\rho}}=\left(K/(1-\zeta),2K/(1-\zeta),\ldots,1\right). For the discretized grid 𝝆¯\bm{\bar{\rho}}, we compute the prior W=Beta​(α,β)W=\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) densities and normalize them, which also gives us the discretized densities for each θai∈𝜽¯𝒂\theta_{a}^{i}\in\bm{\bar{\theta}_{a}} (with i∈(1,2,…,1/K)i\in(1,2,\dots,1/K)):

πα,β,ζ​(θai)=Beta​(θai1−ζ,α,β)∑k=11KBeta​(θak1−ζ,α,β).\pi_{\alpha,\beta,\zeta}(\theta_{a}^{i})=\frac{\text{Beta}(\frac{\theta_{a}^{i}}{1-\zeta};\alpha,\beta)}{\sum_{k=1}^{\frac{1}{K}}\text{Beta}(\frac{\theta_{a}^{k}}{1-\zeta};\alpha,\beta)}.

For all elements of 𝜽¯𝒂\bm{\bar{\theta}_{a}}, the corresponding θb\theta_{b} is retrieved and the likelihood of incoming data points pθa,θb​(Y(j−1))p_{\theta_{a},\theta_{b}}(Y^{(j-1)}) is calculated. We can then estimate the posterior density of θai∈𝜽¯𝒂\theta_{a}^{i}\in\bm{\bar{\theta}_{a}}:

Appendix S3 Type-I error guarantee under optional stopping

Type-I Error

In Figure S3.1 type-I error rates of several 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables and Fisher’s exact test estimated through a simulation experiment are depicted. 20002000 samples of length 10001000 were drawn according to a Bernoulli(0.1)(0.1) distribution to represent 10001000 data streams in two groups. After each complete block m∈{1,…,1000}m\in\{1,\dots,1000\} an 𝙴\mathtt{E}-value or p-value was calculated and the proportion of rejected experiments up until mm with each test type was recorded. As the stream lengths increase, the type-I error rate under (incorrectly applied) optional stopping with Fisher’s exact test increases quickly. The type-I error rate of the 𝙴\mathtt{E}-variables remains bounded.
